## Selection Statements

Selection statements, sometimes referred to as conditional statements,
are one of the three basic constructs (sequence, selection, iteration) in programming.
Selection statements provide the logic to perform decision-making: taking different
actions based on different conditions. When selecting from possible paths for execution,
the decisions are made based on the value of an expression.

C# has the following conditional statements:

- The `if` statement specifies a block of code to be executed, only if a provided Boolean
  expression evaluates to `true`.
- The `if-else` statement allows you to choose which of the two code paths to follow
  based on a Boolean expression.
- The `else if` statement specifies a new `condition` to `test`.
- `switch` statement selects from a list of code to execute based on a pattern match with an expression.

## Boolean Data Type

The condition in an `if` statement is a **Boolean expression** — also called a **relational expression**.
Every expression in C# produces a value, and the defining feature of a Boolean expression is that
its value is always either `true` or `false` (think: Yes/No, On/Off, 1/0).
This two-state result is represented by C#'s `bool` type, whose only legal values are `true` and `false`.

You can quickly try `bool` variables with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or a small VS Code project:

```text
> bool isRollaQuiet = true;
> bool isChicagoClose = false;
> isRollaQuiet
true
> isChicagoClose
false
```

The same Boolean values work directly in a console program. You do not need to define a method or class to try them:

```csharp
bool isRollaQuiet = true;
bool isChicagoClose = false;
Console.WriteLine(isRollaQuiet);
Console.WriteLine(isChicagoClose);
```

The program prints `True` and `False`.

## Boolean Expressions

To drive decision-making in selection statements, Boolean expressions are typically
built using **comparison operators** (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`):

| Operator | Name | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | Relational | Compare numeric (and `char`) values; supported by all integral and floating-point types |
| `==` | Equality | `true` when the compared numbers, characters, Boolean values, or string contents are equal |
| `!=` | Inequality | Opposite of `==` |

Examples:

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(7.0 < 5.1);   // False
Console.WriteLine(7.0 > 5.1);   // True
Console.WriteLine(7.0 <= 5.1);  // False
Console.WriteLine(7.0 >= 5.1);  // True

int a = 1 + 2 + 3;
int b = 6;
Console.WriteLine(a == b);      // True

char c1 = 'a';
char c2 = 'A';
Console.WriteLine(c1 == c2);    // False (different character codes)
```

For the string comparisons used here, `==` compares text contents and is case-sensitive. `"paid"` and `"Paid"` differ. Comparing the identity of custom objects belongs to Chapter 11.

conditional/select statement syntax works:

`false`. The parentheses is a testing construct. If the testing construct results to
`true`, then the code block follows will be executed. Otherwise, the code block
follows will not be executed.

## Logical Operators

To be eligible to graduate from M S&T, you must
have 120 credits *and* a GPA of at least 2.0. C# does not use the
word *and*. Instead it uses `&&` (inherited from the C language).
Then, the requirement translates directly into C# as a *compound condition*
using the logical operator `&&`:

```
credits >= 120 && GPA >=2.0
```

This is true if both `credits >= 120` is true and `GPA >= 2.0`
is true. A short example function using this would be:

The C# syntax for the logical operator `&&` is:

> *condition1* `&&` *condition2*

The compound condition is `true` if `both` of the component conditions
are true. It is `false` if `at least one` of the conditions is false.

Suppose we want a C# condition that is true in the same situations
as the mathematical expression: low < val < high. Unfortunately the
math is not a C# expression. The C# operator `<` is binary.
In C#, the statement above is equivalent to

> (low < val) < high

comparing a Boolean result to high, and causing a compiler error.
There is a C# version. Be sure to use this pattern:

```
low < val && val < high
```

```{index} boolean operator; ||
```

Now suppose we want the opposite condition: that val is *not*
strictly between low and high.
There are several approaches.
One is that `val` would be less than or equal to low
*or* greater than or equal to `high`. C# translate *or* into `||`,
so a C# expression would be:

> val \<= low || val >= high

The C# syntax for the logical operator `||` is:

> *condition1* `||` *condition2*

The compound condition is true if at least one of the component conditions
are true. It is false if both conditions are false.

```{index} boolean operator; !
```

Another logical way to express the opposite of the condition low < val < high
is that it is *not* the case
that low < val && val \<< high. C# translates *not* as `!`. Another way
to state the condition would be

```
!(low < val && val < high)
```

The parentheses are needed because the `!`
operator has higher precedence than
`<`.

A way to remember this strange *not* operator is to think of the use of `!`
in the not-equal operator: `!=`

The C# syntax for the operator `!`:

> `!` *condition*

This whole expression is true when *condition* is false,
and false when *condition* is true.

Because of the precedence of `!`, you are often going to write:

> `!(` *condition* `)`

Remember when such a condition is used in an `if` statement, *outer*
parentheses are also needed:

> `if (!(` *condition* `)) {`

Note that `!` has the high precedence of unary arithmetic operators.
The operators `&&` and `||` are almost at the bottom of the operators
considered in this book, just above the assignment operators, and below the
relational operators, with `&&` above `||`. You are encourages to use
parentheses to make sure.

**Compound Overkill**: Look back to the code converting a score to a letter
grade in the grade-selection example ({ref}`else-if-cases`), the condition before assigning the B
grade could have been:

```
(score >= 80 && score < 90)
```

That would have totally nailed the condition, but it is overly verbose in the
`if` .. `else if` ... code where it appeared. Since you only get
to consider a B as a grade if the grade was *not* already
set to A, the second part of the compound condition above is redundant.

## Compare Ways to Express the Same Decision

An order desk charges 8 for express service, 3 for standard service, and 0 for pickup. This is one rule with mutually exclusive alternatives. An if/else-if chain asks conditions in order and chooses the first true branch. A switch statement selects a matching case. The two forms can implement the same mapping, but choosing a form is not a reason to change the rule.

Start with a decision table before writing either version. Include a value outside the allowed set; otherwise an incomplete program may appear correct merely because all supplied examples happen to name a case.

| Service code | Intended charge | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E | 8 | Express |
| S | 3 | Standard |
| P | 0 | Pickup |
| Anything else | Reject or report an invalid code | No service was selected |

The general statement form is `switch (expression) { case value: statements; break; default: statements; break; }`. This is a syntax pattern, not a complete program. The switch expression is evaluated and matching follows the case rules; `break` leaves the switch. It is not a request to end the application. Modern C# also supports patterns and switch expressions, but those forms are not prerequisites for the basic constant-case statement here.

An if chain is particularly direct when conditions are ranges, such as a quantity below ten or an age above a boundary. A simple constant-case switch reads naturally when one value selects among named alternatives. Do not use three independent if statements when the intended result is exactly one category unless you have established that their tests cannot overlap. An else-if chain communicates that exclusivity directly.

## The `break` Keyword

`break` exits the switch after the selected case. The program then continues with the statement after the switch. C# does not allow ordinary execution to fall through from a nonempty case into the next case. Several case labels can share one body, but simply removing `break` from a nonempty body is not valid.

The `for` statement executes a statement or a block of statements
while a specified **Boolean expression** evaluates to true. Such evaluation involves
comparing the local loop counter variable (an **integer counter** that increments/decrements over every loop)
to a preset value. Since the number of loops is controlled by comparing the counter with the **preset value**,
you need to specify the preset value to decide the number of times you want to run the code block when defining
a `for` loop statement.

## For Statement Syntax

You can see that the `for` loop has four parts, a three-section semicolon-separated **header**
and a **body**:

- **Initializer**: This section is a **variable declaration statement** that
  declares a `local loop variable` (or `iterator variable` or the counter) and initialize it with an initial value.
- **Condition**: The condition section is a **boolean expression** that determines
  if the next iteration in the loop should be executed or should the loop be terminated. If it evaluates to true,
  the next iteration is executed; otherwise, the loop is exited.
- **Iterator**: The iterator (**iteration expression**) section that defines what happens to the counter after each
  execution of the body of the loop. A common behavior is reassigning
  (increment or decrement) the value of the counter.
- The **body** of the loop, which must be a statement or a block of statements.

In the example above, the *initializer* is `i = 1`, *condition* is `i <= n`,
and *iterator* is `i++` (see {ref}`arithmetic operators <arithmetic-operators>`).

Note that the initializer section is executed **only once**, before entering the loop.
Also, the declared variable is local to the `for` loop heading and
the loop body and can not be accessed from outside the for statement.

The two semicolons are always needed in the `for` heading, but any of the
parts they normally separate may be omitted.
If the condition part is omitted, the condition is
interpreted as always true, leading to an infinite loop, that can only
terminate due to a `return` or {ref}`break statement <break-continue>` in the body.

**Header variation**

The declaration of a for loop header is flexible. There may be several variables of the
same type initialized, separated by commas. Also, at the end of the `for` loop heading,
the iteration portion may include more than one expression, also separated by commas.
For example:

for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i = i+2, j++) {

## GCD Example with a `while` Loop

A compact and practical loop example is Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor (GCD):

- Continue while `b != 0`.
- Compute remainder `r = a % b`.
- Shift values: `a = b`, `b = r`.
- When the loop ends, `a` is the GCD.

Just like {ref}`for-statement`, manipulating the header sections will
change the behavior of the loop. This non-terminating example is meant for reading or for a local terminal/VS Code session where you can stop it with `Control + C`:

    > int n = 0;
    > while (n < 5)
    {
       Console.Write(n);
    }
    000000000000000000000000000000...

Observing the code, you see that the variable `n` is not being updated in the body
of the while loop. Since `n` is not updated, the value stays as 0, and the boolean
condition `(n < 5>)` is always evaluated to be `true`, an infinite loop is therefore
formed since (n \< 5) will stay true and, while the boolean condition is tested true, the
body of the while loop will be executed and print out `n`.

If you want the while loop body of the while statement to run at least once, the boolean
condition has to be true for the first evaluation. After that, the iterator (e.g., n++)
in the body of the while statement needs to work to exit the loop by making the condition
section untrue. The preceding code does not have an iterator expression and therefore
the loop becomes infinite.

For comparison, the following `for` statement has the same problem. Treat it as a reading example unless you are testing locally and are ready to stop it with `Control + C`:

    > for (int i = 0; i < 5;)
      {
          Console.Write(i);
      }

After studying the code above, you should have a better idea of how Boolean expressions control loop execution.

**while (true)**

As an exercise, observe the following code. You should be able to see that the condition
section has a value of `true` instead of an expression and reason the outcome of the
code:

    > while (true)
      {
          Console.Write(0);
      }

An infinite loop can happen when:

1.  The loop has no terminating condition.
2.  The loop has a terminating condition that cannot be met.

An embedded system such as a cartridge-based video game console typically does not
have an `exit` condition and the loop runs until the console is powered off. The
same infinite loop design can be seen in operating systems or web servers, where the
systems keep monitor input and give output and do not halt until crash, turned off,

An important feature of functions/methods is that they can **return** values to their
**callers**. In the example below, `SquareTheNumber(int num)` is defined with a return type of `int`
and is called directly from the top-level code, passing a parameter.

In this example:

- `return num * num;` computes the value that replaces this call in the caller.
- `digit` starts at 4. Passing it binds the value 4 to `num`.
- `squaredNum` is a variable, not a method; it stores the returned 16.
- The addition uses `squaredNum` plus a second call with digit still equal to 4: 16 + 16 = 32.
- The final call uses 5 and returns 25. The three printed values are 16, 32, and 25.

The return type must agree with the returned expression through an allowed conversion. `void` means no returned value; it does not mean the method cannot print or have another effect.

## Flow of execution

In terms of the construct of **sequential processing**, functions/methods
alter code execution order in several ways: by statements not
being executed as the definition is first read, and then when the
method is called during execution, jumping to the method code,
and back at the end of the method execution. [^0502_signature_call-5]

A class can contain multiple methods. It can be tempting to think the
methods are executed in the order they appear in the class, but this is
not the case. In an explicit class-based console program, ordinary execution begins in the selected Main method; a top-level program begins with its first statement. Each statement in the main is executed sequentially, one at a
time, until you reach a method call. A method call causes the program
execution to jump to the first line of the called method.
Each statement in the called method is then executed in order.
When the called method finishes, execution returns to the point in its caller that was waiting for the result. The caller may itself be another helper. [^0502_signature_call-6]

In other words, the order in which the method definition code blocks does
not matter to C#. It is a human choice. One good practice is to show
`Main` first. This means a human reading in order gets an overview
of what is happening by looking at Main, but does not know the details
until reading the definitions of other methods.

## Method definition

The general syntax for defining a static method is:

```csharp
static returnTypeOrVoid MethodName ( parameter_list )
{
   // statements in the method body...
}
```

Things to know about defining a method in C#:

1. **Parameters**: The *parameter list* can be empty or contain one or more comma separated parameter entries. Each parameter entry has the form 
   > type parameterName

2. **Modifier**: For class-member methods, accessibility determines which callers are permitted. `public static` allows access through the type where that type is accessible; other access levels have other rules. Local helpers beside top-level statements do not take an access modifier.

3. **Return Type**: If **returnTypeOrVoid** in the heading is not `void`, each normally completing path must produce a compatible result; the mere presence of one return statement is insufficient. A return statement has the form

   > `return` *expression* `;`

   where the expression should be of the same type as in **returnTypeOrVoid**.
   Execution of the method terminates immediately when a return statement
   is reached.

4. In the traditional class-based style, execution starts at a method with a heading including

   > `static void Main`

   In modern C#, programs may also use *top-level statements* without an explicit `Main` method.

## Method Calls

1. A method call takes the form

   **MethodName** `(` actual parameter list `)`

   A method call makes the method definition be *executed*.

2. The actual parameter list is a comma separated list of the *same*
   length as the parameter list. Each entry is an expression.
   The entries in an actual parameter list do *not* include type declarations.

   Effectively, the method execution starts by assigning to each
   parameter variable the corresponding value from
   evaluating the actual parameter expression.
   In particular, that means the actual parameter values must be allowed
   in an assignment statement for a variable of the parameter's type!

3. If the method has return type `void`, it can only be used syntactically
   as an entire statement (with a semicolon added). After the method
   call completes, execution continues with the next statement.

4. If there is a non-void return type, then the method call is syntactically
   an expression in the statement where it appears.
   The execution of such a method must reach a return statement. The value
   of the method-call expression is the value of the expression in this
   return statement.

5. A method with a return value can also legally be used as a whole statement.
   In this case the return value is lost. Though legal, this is often an error!

## Variable Scopes

A variable may be available for use in some parts of code, but not others.
The `scope` of a variable is the region of the program that the variable is visible,
which means it is accessible by `name` and can be used in the part of code. C# scope rules of variables can be divided into three categories as follows:

- Class Level Scope
- Method Level Scope
- Block Level Scope.

A variable declared inside a method is a `local variable`. A body local belongs to its containing block; a parameter is available in the method body. A nested-block local cannot be used outside that block. You cannot use a local variable before its declaration or read it before it has a value.
In the ordinary noncapturing examples here, each call has its own local values. Do not infer a physical memory address or allocation rule from a scope diagram.
If you called the method again, the old value is not available.

Only the *value* of the actual parameter is passed, not any
variable name, so there is *no need* to have a match between a variable name
(arguments) and the parameter name.

| Region | What can use its local name? | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parameter | The called method body | It belongs to this call. |
| Method-body local | Its containing scope after declaration | Another method cannot read it just because it uses the same spelling. |
| Nested block local | That block after declaration | Moving its use outside the block is a compile-time error. |

Scope concerns where a name can be used in source code; lifetime concerns the duration of a value/storage relationship. The later chapters have cases requiring deeper lifetime analysis. Here use separate boxes for caller and helper locals rather than claiming the compiler must allocate/release a specific memory location at each brace.

The output is `Caller x: 1; returned y: 8`. The helper's x does not overwrite the caller's x. A static local helper cannot capture the caller's local x; it receives a through its parameter. If a name is needed after a block, declare it in an appropriate enclosing scope and decide how it is initialized, rather than assuming any earlier variable remains available everywhere.

A return value is usually the clearest way to produce one result. Sometimes a method must report both success and a result, or deliberately update a caller variable. C# makes those effects explicit with `out` and `ref`. This connects the `TryParse` call in Chapter 4 to the method definitions you can now write.

General definition and call patterns (schematic):

```csharp
static bool TryRead(string text, out int value) { /* assign value on every normal return */ }
bool success = TryRead(text, out number);
static void Adjust(ref int value) { /* read or replace caller value */ }

| Parameter | Caller obligation | Method obligation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int value` | Supply a value. | Works with a local copy. | Reassignment does not replace the caller variable. |
| `out int value` | Supply a writable variable, not necessarily initialized. | Assign it before every normal return. | Produces a result in the caller variable. |
| `ref int value` | Supply an initialized writable variable. | May read and replace it. | Deliberately shares the caller variable's storage. |

## Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question

A report says that three expense entries, 12, 8 and 5, total 20. Saying that the total is wrong identifies a symptom, but it does not yet locate the defect. First derive the expected total independently: 12 + 8 + 5 is 25. Keep the three inputs fixed. A changing input set makes it difficult to tell whether a code change repaired the problem or merely avoided it.

Suppose the program loops while index is less than the number of entries minus one. The loop body may contain correct addition and still omit the final item. This is why debugging begins with the contract and a concrete failing case rather than rewriting whichever line looks suspicious. ## Test a Hypothesis Against Execution

State a hypothesis before stepping: perhaps the loop visits only two entries. Put a breakpoint before the loop, not after the incorrect report has already been produced. Observe index, the current input, and the accumulated total. Step over the update, then watch the loop condition. In VS Code, a breakpoint pauses execution when the running program reaches that source location; it does not itself execute or repair the line. Step Into follows a call, while Step Over completes that call without opening its internal steps.

| Observation point | Index being processed | Total after the update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First iteration | 0 | 12 |
| Second iteration | 1 | 20 |
| Expected third iteration | 2 | 25 |

If execution never reaches the third row, the evidence supports an iteration-boundary defect. If all three updates occur but the final result is still 20, investigate later reassignment or output instead. A useful observation distinguishes competing explanations. Repeatedly pressing Step without a question can produce many observations without improving understanding.

The call stack tells you how execution reached the paused method. Local variables belong to the current call; selecting another frame can show another call's values. A watch expression is a view of a value, not proof that the value satisfies a business rule. Prefer observations that do not alter program state. A debugging expression that invokes a mutating method can itself change the behavior you are trying to understand.

## Introduction

The purpose of testing in software development is to establish developer’s confidence that the
code continues to have high quality and less errors, hence to ensure that the requirements of
the project are met.

Testing is a critical part of software development. In JetBrain’s The State of
Developer Ecosystem 2023 survey [1], for example, 80% of the
respondents say that “testing plays an integral role in their software development
projects.” Also, 63% of respondents say they use **Unit testing** in their projects while
47% say they use Integration testing.

It is also noteworthy that while 41% of respondents say they have less
than 1 tester/Quality Assurance Engineer per 10 developers, 32% of the respondents say
that they have 1-3 testers/QA per 10 software developers. Testing, especially unit testing,
therefore, is a common practice in real world software development.

Amazon AWS defines unit testing as:

> Unit testing is the process where you test the smallest functional unit of code.
> Software testing helps ensure code quality, and it’s an integral part of software
> development. It’s a software development best practice to write software as small,
> functional units then write a unit test for each code unit. You can first write
> unit tests as code. Then, run that test code automatically every time you make
> changes in the software code. This way, if a test fails, you can quickly isolate
> the area of the code that has the bug or error. Unit testing enforces modular
> thinking paradigms and improves test coverage and quality. Automated unit
> testing helps ensure you or your developers have more time to concentrate on coding. [2]

The notion of unit testing is straightforward in principle. When you write a program
in general, the program comprises what are properly known as units of development.
Each language has its own definition of what units are but most modern programming
languages view the **class** concept as the core unit of testing, although it can be done
at lower level such as **method** and higher level such as package. Once we have a class,
we can test it and all of the parts associated with it, especially its methods.

Unit testing is usually done by using testing frameworks. For C#, popular testing
frameworks include: MSTest, NUnit, and xUnit.

We have explored several ways of storing a collection of the same type of data:

- arrays: built-in syntax, unchanging size of the collection
- List: generic class type, allows the size of the collection to grow

Both approaches allow reference to data elements using a
numerical index between square brackets, as in `words[i]`.
The index provides an order for the elements,
but there is no meaning to the index beyond the sequence order.

Sometimes, we want to look up data based on a more meaningful key, as in a
dictionary: given a word, you can look up the definition.

C# uses the type name [Dictionary](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.dictionary-2?view=net-8.0), but with greater generality than in
nontechnical use. In a regular dictionary, you start with a word,
and look up the definition. The generalization is to have some piece of
data that leads you to (or *maps* to) another piece of data.
The computer science jargon is that a **key** leads you to a **value**.
In a normal dictionary, these are both likely to be strings, but in the
C# generalization, the possible types of key and value are much more extensive.
Hence the generic `Dictionary` type requires you to specify
*both a type for the key and a type for the value*.

A stock clerk knows a product code, not its position in a list. Searching for that code and coordinating a separate quantity list is unnecessary work when the program can directly associate the code with its quantity. The big idea is a **key-to-value association**. Retrieval, updating stock, and counting repeated requests all reuse that association.

Keep three questions separate: Is the key present? What value belongs to it? Does this operation insert a new entry or update an existing one? Keys identify entries; they are not sequence positions. The examples below retain the translation dictionary, then transfer the same pattern to counting.

In most real world scenarios, especially in business settings, operations carried
out with computers and information systems usually involve data processing and
may generate new data as a result. To make the data *persistent* past the end of
program execution, data are stored in file system or databases (for structured data). Although a
database maybe preferred in many cases, there will be times that you need to read and write files
for various purposes.

A file is a collection of data stored on in a storage device with a name and
directory path information. A file is stored in your file system, which is part of
the operating system (OS), and the OS therefore has the information about the file
and how to access it.

## File Stream

In .NET, file and stream I/O (input/output) refers to the transfer of data either to or from a
storage medium. The System.IO namespaces contain types that enable reading and writing,
both synchronously and asynchronously, on data streams and files, in addition to other file and stream operations.

You have already read and written streams of
characters to the `Console`. Most of the syntax that we use for files will be very similar, using
methods `ReadLine`, `WriteLine`, and `Write` in the same way you used them for the `Console`.

When you read/write a file in C# program, the data processed is seen as a **Stream**.
A stream is a sequence of bytes of data sent between the destination and the source of
the file. Streams are how data is read and written to and from files, networks, and
computer memory. For example, printing data using a printer involves sending a sequence
of bytes of data to a stream associated with a network port connected to the printer.

### File handling process

For file handling operations, there are two obvious streams:

1.  The **Input Stream** that is used to read data from a file (read operation).
2.  The **Output Stream** that is used to write data into a file (write operation).

However, different task processes use different type of streams: text files, binary files,
strings, and network communications are some of the examples. The basic
stream operations therefore include the following:

1.  Creation/Opening
2.  Reading
3.  Writing
4.  Positioning
5.  Closing

### The `System.IO` namespace

Files can be handled very differently by different operating systems, but
C# abstracts away the differences and provides stream interfaces between
a C# program and files through the `System.IO namespace` ({ref}`namespace <namespace>`). The System.IO namespace

about file and directory structure.

is one of the classes that provides static methods for the creation, copying, deletion, moving, and

## Separate a File's Location from Its Contents

A report can contain perfectly valid text and still fail to open because its path names the wrong location. A relative path is interpreted from the process's working directory, which need not be the directory containing the source file. Before changing your parsing code, establish which file the program is actually trying to open.

The resource workflow is a sequence: choose the location, acquire the resource, process data, and release the resource. Reading and writing are separate contracts. Overwriting a report, appending a new entry, and reading an existing log are not interchangeable operations just because they share a path.

| Question | Example consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Is the path relative or absolute? | Running from another working directory can select another file |
| Must the file already exist? | A missing input is different from a new output |
| May existing contents be replaced? | Opening the wrong write mode can destroy a previous report |
| Who owns the open resource? | Cleanup must occur even if processing stops early |

Use Path.Combine to assemble path components for the current platform rather than hard-coding one separator convention. This constructs a path string; it does not create directories, grant permissions, or prove that an input file exists. Likewise, checking existence before opening cannot guarantee that a later open succeeds: resource state can change between those operations.

## Bound Resource Lifetime Explicitly

A StreamReader or StreamWriter owns resources that must be disposed. A using statement or declaration expresses that lifetime. The general declaration form is `using ResourceType name = acquisitionExpression;`; this is a syntax pattern. Processing statements use that acquired resource inside its permitted scope. Disposal handles resource release; it does not establish that every record was valid or that a business transaction completed successfully.

For an input import, distinguish two outcomes: the resource cannot be opened, or a particular line has invalid data. The first may prevent the whole import. The second may permit recording the line number and continuing, if that is the stated policy. Do not catch an unavailable-file exception and silently report that zero valid records were found; zero records and no readable input are different outcomes.

## Path Strings

When a program is running, there is alway a *current directory* (or,
**present working directory**, `pwd`). Files in the present working directory can
be referred to by their simple names, e.g., *sample.txt*, so
project files can be referred to by their simple names because they are in the same
directory.

Referring to files not in the current directory is more complicated.
You should be aware from using the Windows Explorer or the macOS Finder that
files and directories are located in a hierarchy of directories in the
file system. On a Mac, the file system is unified in
one hierarchy. On Windows, each storage drive has its own hierarchy.

```{index} path separator
```

Files are generally referred to by a chain of directories before
the final name of the file desired. A *path string* (or simply **path**) is used
to represent such a sequence of names. Elements of the directory chain are separated
by operating system specific punctuation symbols: In Windows the separator is
backslash, `\`, and on a Mac it is (forward) slash, `/`. For example, on a Mac the path

```none
/Users/anh
```

starts with a /, meaning the **root** or top directory in the hierarchy, and Users is
a subdirectory, and anh is a subdirectory of Users (in this case the home directory
for the user with login anh). It is similar with Windows, except there may be a drive
in the beginning, and the separator is a \\, so

```none
C:\Windows\System32
```

is on C: drive; Windows is a subdirectory of the root directory \\, and System32 is
a subdirectory of Windows. Each drive in Windows has a separate file hierarchy
underneath it.

```{index} path; absolute
```

Paths starting from the root of a file system, with `\` or `/` are called
**absolute paths** or **full paths** because they begin with the root of the file hierarchy.
Since there is always a current directory, it makes sense to allow a path to be *relative*
to the current directory. In that case do *not* start with the slash that would
indicate the root directory. For example, if the current directory is

## Paths in C\#

The differing versions of paths for Windows and a Mac are a pain to deal with. Luckily C#
abstracts away the differences. It has a `Path` class in the `System.IO`

## Overview

To understand class and object-oriented programming (OOP), some important basic concepts learn first inlcude:

- **Class**: A class is a blueprint, prototype, or template.
- **Class Members**: In C#, a class contains members, which include **fields**, properties, **methods**, and events.
- **Class Instance**: An `object` is an `instance` of a class. Namely, an object is created based on a
  class and therefore is an instance of that class. An object can be created using the `new` keyword.

There are related terminology that you will see about class and OOP:

- **Field**: A field is a variable of any type that is declared directly in a class or struct. Fields are
  members of their containing type. A field stores a piece of data within an object. It acts like a
  variable and may have a different value for each instance of a type. [1]
- **Property**: Properties expose fields. Fields should (almost always) be kept private to a class and accessed via
  get and set properties.
- The **this** Keyword: In C#, the this keyword refers to the current instance of a class.
- **Reference Types**: A type that is defined as a class is a reference type. Other types include: interface, struct, delegate, or enum.
- **Constructor**: In C#, a constructor is called when an object is created to set default values. A constructor must have the
  **same name** as the enclosing class. Using constructor is not obligatory in C#. If no constructors are specified in a class, the compiler
  automatically creates a parameterless constructor.

## A Variable Number of Arguments

```{index} gap revision: a variable number of arguments
```

An invoice may contain zero, one, or several charges. Writing a separate `Sum` overload for every possible number of charges does not scale. A parameter array lets one method receive those arguments as an array. It connects familiar array traversal to a more convenient calling form.

General pattern (schematic):

```csharp
static decimal Sum(params decimal[] amounts) { /* process amounts */ }
```

`params` marks the final parameter. In this array form, callers can supply separate compatible values, an existing array, or no values. Inside the method, `amounts` is still an array with a length. The keyword does not mean that one call returns multiple answers. An empty call supplies an empty array; decide explicitly what the method should return for it.

Overloads share a method name but have different parameter lists. For example, `Sum(decimal a, decimal b)` and `Sum(decimal[] amounts)` are distinct overloads, while a changed return type alone cannot distinguish them. A parameter array often avoids a family of repetitive fixed-arity overloads. Keep the simple array form here; broader overload and polymorphism choices are developed later.

See the language/API reference for this contract.[^gap-params]

## Separate Location Cost from Update Cost

A service desk stores `n` work orders. Two requests that sound similar can require different work: “insert at position 400” supplies an index; “insert after this node” supplies a location handle. Compare the same request and the same assumptions before claiming a speed advantage.

| Request | Dynamic array | Singly linked list with head and tail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read index i | O(1) | O(i + 1), O(n) worst case |
| Append | O(1) amortized, O(n) on resize | O(1) with stored tail |
| Insert at front | O(n) shifts | O(1) |
| Insert by index in middle | O(n) shifts, possibly growth | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove by index in middle | O(n) shifts | O(n) locate, O(1) rewire |
| Remove last | O(1), without shrinking | O(n) find predecessor |
| Search unsorted values | O(n) | O(n) |
| Visit every item once | O(n) | O(n) with cursor |

The linked wrapper in this chapter exposes indices rather than public node handles. Its middle insertion therefore includes traversal. A different API could expose validated handles, but it must specify ownership and what happens when a handle refers to a removed node.

## Count a Concrete Workload

Use eight initial orders and spare array capacity. Compare a front insertion, a last-position read, and a front removal.

| Operation | Array work | Linked work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert at front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |
| Read last position after insertion | One indexed read | Eight link advances from head |
| Remove front | Eight existing-value shifts | No link traversal; update head |

If readers request the last position 100 times between these updates, the array uses 100 indexed reads while the linked sequence uses 800 link advances. If the workload instead performs many front updates and few index reads, the preference may reverse. Include the whole operation mix.

Counts of different primitives are not interchangeable seconds. Copying a reference, following a link, allocating a node, and checking a bound have different costs. Counts explain how work grows; benchmarks answer a narrower question about a specific implementation and machine.

## Test the Contract Before Comparing Speed

Both implementations should produce the same logical result for the same legal operation sequence. Test correctness first. A fast implementation that loses an order is not an alternative representation of the same ADT.

| Test | Operations | Expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empty start | Construct | Count zero; read index zero throws. |
| Single element | Add A; remove index zero | Returns A; count zero. |
| Reuse after emptying | Previous test; add B | Read index zero returns B. |
| Middle insertion | Add A, C; insert B at one | A, B, C in that order. |
| Middle removal | Previous test; remove one | Returns B; leaves A, C. |
| Duplicate values | Add A twice; remove zero | One A remains. |
| Invalid insertion | Insert at count plus one | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |
| Invalid removal | Remove at count | Throws; count and contents unchanged. |

Do not test only printed output from the happy path. Check count after each operation, and verify remaining values after removal. A useful additional check compares a generated operation sequence against C# `List<T>` as a reference implementation. It does not make timing comparisons fair; it checks observable behavior.

## Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation

For `int` elements, the backing array places the integer values together. For reference-type elements, the reference slots are contiguous but their target objects need not be. Sequential array access often benefits from memory locality. A linked traversal follows separately allocated node objects, which may be scattered in memory.

Linked lists also pay for a node object and link field per item. Dynamic arrays pay for spare capacity and occasional replacement arrays. Neither representation has universally smaller memory usage: the element type, spare capacity, object layout, and workload matter.

Begin with a dynamic array such as `List<T>` for ordinary indexed application sequences. Justify a linked structure when its operations and API offer a concrete benefit, such as repeated front removal or insertion at already known positions. Do not replace every `List<T>` just because some linked updates have constant cost.

## Summary

Arrays and linked lists both represent sequences, but they optimize different operations. A strong data-structure choice starts with the workload: what the program does most often, what must be fast, and what tradeoffs are acceptable.

## Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors

A delivery graph has edges A-B, A-C, B-D and C-D. Starting at A, how many roads are needed to reach each stop? Breadth-first search answers a minimum-hop question in an unweighted graph. It keeps a queue of discovered vertices whose outgoing neighbors still need examination. Discovery and processing are different events: a vertex can already be known while it is still waiting in the queue.

Mark a vertex discovered when it is enqueued. If you wait until dequeue, both B and C can enqueue D before D is processed. That duplicates work and makes predecessor choices harder to reason about. A visited/discovered set is therefore part of the algorithm's state, not merely an optional speed optimization.

| Processing event | Queue afterward | Newly discovered distances |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initialize A | A | A: 0 |
| Examine A | B, C | B: 1, C: 1 |
| Examine B | C, D | D: 2 |
| Examine C | D | None; D is already known |
| Examine D | Empty | None |

The table assumes that A lists B before C. A different neighbor order can choose another equally short predecessor route, but it does not change the minimum hop distance. Tests that insist on one exact path without specifying neighbor order can reject correct results. State the tie policy separately from the distance claim.

## Recover a Path from Earlier Layers

When discovering a new vertex v from u, record predecessor[v] = u and distance[v] = distance[u] + 1. Following those predecessor links backward reconstructs a route to the source. Reverse the route to display it from source to destination. The source is a one-vertex route to itself; an unreachable known vertex has no source route. Do not fabricate a destination-only path when no predecessor chain exists.

Why is the distance minimal? The queue processes vertices in nondecreasing discovered distance. All one-hop vertices are discovered from the source before processing can expose a two-hop successor, and the same reasoning repeats layer by layer. The first discovery therefore uses a shortest hop count. This reasoning relies on equal edge contribution, not on geometric closeness or vertex spelling. With arbitrary weights, fewer edges can be more expensive; Chapter 24 treats that different objective.

For adjacency lists, visiting reachable vertices and their incident/outgoing entries costs work proportional to those entries plus vertex bookkeeping. A traversal of one component does not visit all disconnected components by magic. If the task is a full undirected component report, start a new traversal from each still-undiscovered vertex, including isolates.

## Watch the Suspended Neighbor Loop

Depth-first search is ordinary recursive control flow applied to a graph. A call must remember which neighbor it is considering while a child explores its branch. This connects the suspended calls in Chapter 17 to Chapter 20's cycles and shared destinations. A discovered set avoids repeated discovery; it does not erase the caller's unfinished neighbor loop.

Use the undirected diamond A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, and isolated E. In each array below, the listed neighbor order determines the trace. Watch enter and exit events separately. A vertex is entered once; returning from a child resumes an already active parent rather than entering that parent again.

Enter B depth 1
Enter D depth 2
Enter C depth 3
Exit C
Exit D
Exit B
Exit A

source:
C is first entered from D, not from A. A's neighbor loop has not finished, but C is already discovered by the time A resumes and considers it. C's DFS depth is three although A has a direct edge to C. A first DFS route therefore need not minimize hops.

| Event | Active frames from oldest to newest | What waits in the caller? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enter A | A | A will consider C after B returns |
| Enter B | A,B | B will finish after D returns |
| Enter D | A,B,D | D will finish after C returns |
| Enter C | A,B,D,C | C finds no undiscovered neighbor |
| Exit C | A,B,D | D resumes its neighbor loop |
| Exit D | A,B | B resumes |
| Exit B | A | A sees that C is already discovered |
| Exit A | Empty | Source traversal is complete |

Do not use the number of discovered vertices as the current stack depth. Four vertices have been discovered after C exits, but only three calls remain active at that point. Likewise, a visited neighbor alone is not enough to classify a directed cycle: completed and active destinations have different meanings.

## Finish One Branch Before Returning to Its Alternatives

Depth-first search follows an unvisited neighbor, completes the exploration reachable through that choice, and then returns to the caller's remaining neighbors. The control pattern connects to tree traversal, but a graph can have shared destinations and cycles. A discovered set prevents following those connections forever.

Use A with neighbors B and C, B connected to D, and C also connected to D. With B considered first, a recursive DFS can enter A, B, D and then C if the adjacency order supplies that route. When the call from D has completed, execution resumes in the suspended neighbor loop of its caller. A plain stack of vertices can provide a valid depth-first exploration policy, but reproducing exact recursive entry/exit timing requires storing enough progress to know which neighbor a suspended frame should consider next.

| Event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Enter a new vertex | Mark discovered; begin its neighbor sequence |
| Encounter an already discovered vertex | Avoid a second discovery; interpret the edge under the graph model |
| Return from a child | Resume the parent's remaining neighbors |
| Exit a vertex | Its chosen neighbor sequence is complete |

Do not infer a directed cycle merely from seeing an edge to any previously visited vertex. That destination might already have completed. Directed-cycle reasoning distinguishes an active unfinished path from completed exploration. In an undirected graph, the edge back to the parent also needs special treatment. A single Boolean visited flag solves repeated discovery; additional state or parent information may be needed for the specific cycle question.

## Connectivity Depends on Direction

For a symmetric undirected adjacency model, repeated traversals from undiscovered vertices partition the graph into connected components. Every vertex belongs to exactly one such component, and an isolated vertex forms a component by itself. Directed reachability is not symmetric: A may reach B even when B cannot reach A. Repeating ordinary forward searches in arbitrary order does not automatically compute strongly connected components.

Verification can check that each discovered vertex enters/exits once, parent-child call intervals are nested under the recursive model, and every reported reachable vertex has a path from the source. It should not assume that DFS yields minimum-hop paths. BFS has that guarantee under its unweighted model; DFS's first route may be longer.

Guided comparison: draw a graph where A connects directly to D but also begins a long chain that eventually reaches D. Process the chain neighbor first. Predict a DFS route and a BFS route. Then reverse one edge in the chain and identify which reachability claims must be reconsidered. Explain the observed difference using the frontier policy and edge directions rather than the generic phrase graph search.

```{index} Depth-First Search and Cycles
```

Depth-first search (DFS) follows a branch before returning to another neighbor. Mark before following neighbors: a cycle then leads to an already visited vertex rather than infinite recursion. This teaching implementation uses recursive calls; the runtime call stack records unfinished work. It can require O(V) stack space and very deep graphs may exceed runtime stack limits. Part VII develops further traversal techniques. DFS discovers reachability, but its discovery depth does not promise a shortest route.

## Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion

Assume two input runs are already sorted under the same policy. To merge them, compare their first unread elements and choose the smaller. No later element in either run can be smaller than that run's first unread element, so the chosen value is safe as the next output. Recursion supplies sorted runs; it does not remove the need to justify this combining rule.

Merge [2, 5] with [1, 5, 7]. Choose 1 from the right, then 2 from the left. At the tie between the two 5 values, choosing the left one first preserves relative order when these runs came from adjacent parts of the original input. After one run is exhausted, copy the remaining suffix of the other; it is already sorted.

| Output so far | Left unread | Right unread |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [] | 2, 5 | 1, 5, 7 |
| [1] | 2, 5 | 5, 7 |
| [1, 2] | 5 | 5, 7 |
| [1, 2, 5-left] | Empty | 5-right, 7 |

The invariant combines ordering and preservation: output contains exactly the consumed input occurrences in sorted order, and its final element is no greater than the remaining candidates. Keeping only the ordering claim would not rule out accidentally duplicating one occurrence and losing another.

Range/buffer implementations add an indexing obligation. Source and destination ranges must refer to the intended segments; copying into the wrong offset can produce correct tiny whole-array results and fail on an interior range. Trace a merge whose lo is not zero, and include odd lengths. A reusable buffer can reduce allocation without changing the merge contract.

Guided verification: label equal invoice amounts with original IDs. Check that sorted order holds, every original ID occurs exactly once, and equal-key IDs retain their arrival order. Then compare a nonmutating sort that returns a fresh outer array with an in-place sort. Both may order values correctly, but only one satisfies a contract that preserves the caller's original array order.

For related explanation, see the further reading below.[^development-reading]

```{index} Combining Sorted Parts
```

## Combining Sorted Parts
```{index} Combining Sorted Parts
Merge sort depends on a combine step called **merge**. Given two sorted arrays, merge walks through both arrays and builds one sorted result.

Merge requires two inputs sorted under the same comparison, and returns a fresh sorted array containing every input occurrence. At the main loop head, k=i+j and result[0,k) is the stable sorted merge of the consumed prefixes. The next smallest unconsumed item must be at one of the two fronts. Choosing the left front on equality preserves original order. Once one side is exhausted, copy the other remainder without further comparisons. For total N>0, merging takes Θ(N) time/output space and at most N−1 key comparisons; empty sides can need zero comparisons but still require copying.

```{index} Merge Sort
```

## Merge Sort
```{index} Merge Sort
Merge sort divides the array into halves until each piece has zero or one item, then merges sorted pieces back together.

The copy-returning contract leaves the input unchanged and returns a fresh array even for zero or one item. Slices allocate new arrays, making this version easy to read but allocation-heavy. T(n)=T(floor(n/2))+T(ceil(n/2))+Θ(n), so time is Θ(n log n) for n≥2. Stack depth is Θ(log n). The next section replaces slices with index ranges and a reusable buffer; it also verifies stability and preservation. Comparisons are only one part of sorting cost: copying still happens when a side is exhausted.

```{index} Design Checklist
```

## Design Checklist
```{index} Design Checklist

When designing a divide-and-conquer algorithm, ask:

1. What is the smallest case I can solve directly?
2. How do I divide the input?
3. Do I solve one subproblem or multiple subproblems?
4. How do I combine the answers?
5. What recurrence describes the cost?

## Trace Merge Fronts
```{index} Trace Merge Fronts
Track consumed indexes i and j and output index k. Equal keys take the left item first. Predict which side runs out, then trace both the comparison loop and the tail copies.

The invariant k=i+j and sorted consumed-prefix merge explains why no value disappears. The measure (left.Length−i)+(right.Length−j) decreases after every copy. Stability is relative to a comparison key; equal integer values cannot display record order, so use labeled invoices next.

```{index} Sort Ranges with One Buffer
```

## Sort Ranges with One Buffer
```{index} Sort Ranges with One Buffer

The public method clones the input once and allocates one reusable buffer. SortRange(start,end) sorts a half-open range. Sibling calls finish sequentially, then merge their sorted ranges into the matching buffer range and copy back. Counts reset at each Sort call.

Assume each recursive call correctly sorts its smaller range and preserves its items. The merge invariant establishes the same promise for the parent. Empty/singleton ranges return directly. Odd lengths are fully covered. The copied output and buffer use Θ(n) storage, and the stack adds Θ(log n); total auxiliary space is Θ(n). Across all levels there are Θ(n log n) writes, but cumulative writes are not peak memory. The original slice version also allocates across levels; separate total allocation volume from peak live storage.

```{index} Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
```

## Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices
```{index} Verify Stability with Labeled Invoices

A stable sort preserves arrival order among equal amounts. Compare only the amount, and track identity separately. A consistent comparison must define an ordering; subtracting integer keys can overflow, so use CompareTo.

Changing the merge comparison from ≤0 to <0 would let equal right items overtake equal left items. Stability matters when reports preserve earlier arrival order or apply successive sorts. It is a property of the algorithm and comparison policy, not merely of sorted numeric output.

```{index} Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
```

## Check Order, Preservation, and Copying
```{index} Check Order, Preservation, and Copying

Sortedness alone is insufficient: returning an empty array is sorted but loses every invoice. Compare against an independent sorted reference, check input preservation and array identity, and include empty, singleton, odd, duplicate, reverse, negative, and extreme cases.

```{index} Compare Measured Operations
```

## Compare Measured Operations
```{index} Compare Measured Operations

Count actual key comparisons and element writes. The asymptotic expression n log₂ n is a growth model, not an exact comparison count. Different orders can exhaust one merge side earlier. Buffer copy-back contributes writes even after comparisons stop.

For powers of two, this implementation performs exactly 2n log₂ n counted writes: one buffer write and one copy-back write per item per internal level. Clone and buffer allocation are setup and are excluded from that counter, but included in the algorithm’s overall cost. Recursion has 2n−1 calls for nonempty input. Time remains Θ(n log n); these are deterministic operation counts, not timings.

## The Microsoft Language and .NET Ecosystem

Before installing tools, it helps to know where C# sits. **.NET** is Microsoft's free, open-source platform for building many kinds of applications. It runs programs written in several languages, and it provides **app stacks**: libraries and templates for a particular kind of application. The tools you install in this section serve the whole platform, not only this course.

| Language | Role today | In this course |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C#** | Microsoft's most widely used .NET language; most of .NET itself is written in it | The language you learn |
| **F#** | Functional-first language, used for data-heavy and analytical code | Not covered |
| **Visual Basic** | Maintained for stability and C# interoperability, not receiving new features | Not covered |
| **C++/CLI** | Legacy bridge between C++ and .NET; Windows-only and maintained for compatibility | Not covered |

## Connections, Commands, and Disposal

```

A `SqliteConnection` opens the local database. A command holds SQL text and parameters. A reader steps through result rows. `using` disposes each resource when its scope ends, including when an exception leaves the scope. This `using` declaration manages a resource; it has a different role from a namespace import.

The reference project follows this order: open a connection, enable foreign keys, create tables, seed missing sample records, construct an `Inventory`, and request operations. Inspect the setup before the class definitions in `Program.cs`.

## Map Rows to Objects

```{index} Map Rows to Objects
```

`Book` groups an ID, title, price in cents, and stock. `Inventory.List` uses an explicit column order and reads each row into a new `Book`. `Find` returns either one book or `null`; missing data is an expected result, not automatically an exception.

Read `ReadBook` and match every reader position to its selected column. Predict what could go wrong if a query changed column order without updating the mapper. Keep each command's result shape explicit.

## Supply Parameters and Check Outcomes

```{index} Supply Parameters and Check Outcomes
```

`Add` passes the title, price, and stock as values. A count of delivered packages is a whole number; a quoted price may need decimal fractions; a product code is text even when it consists of digits. Choosing a type is therefore a modeling decision, not a search for the smallest box that happens to fit today's example. Start with the allowed values and operations. ## Types

In C#, **everything is a type**. Every value you store, every variable you declare, and every expression you write has a type. A **type** defines three things:

- **Value**: The **set of valid values** it can hold (e.g., `int` holds whole numbers −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647).
- **Operation**: The **operations** permitted on those values (e.g., arithmetic on numbers, `.Length` on strings).
- **Memory**: The **amount of memory** reserved when a variable of that type is created.

C# types split into two fundamental categories: **value types** and **reference types**. The difference between them is not just a classification detail — it changes what happens when you assign one variable to another, which is worth seeing directly before anything else.

```{index} type system; value type; reference type
```

### The Type System: Value, Reference, void, and Defaults

Every specific type you will meet in this book — `int`, `string`, an array, a class you write yourself — is an instance of a small number of umbrella concepts. Learning those umbrella concepts first means every new type you meet afterward already has a slot to fit into, instead of feeling like a fresh, unrelated fact. This section covers four of them: the value/reference split that governs assignment, `void` (the type that means "no value"), and default values (what a variable holds before you give it one).

```{index} value type
```

#### Value Types

A variable of a **value type** directly contains its data. Value types include the numeric primitives (`int`, `double`, `long`, and the rest), `bool`, `char`, and user-defined `struct` and `enum` types. Despite their keyword status, each built-in value type is simply an alias for a .NET struct in the `System` namespace — `int` is `System.Int32`, `bool` is `System.Boolean`.[^0201_variables_types-types-ref]

Assigning one value-type variable to another **copies the value**. The two variables are then completely independent — changing one never affects the other:

```{index} reference type
```

#### Reference Types

A variable of a **reference type** does not hold its data directly — it holds a reference (an address) pointing to where the data actually lives. Reference types include `class`, `interface`, `delegate`, and `record`; `string` and `object` are the two built-in reference types.

Assigning one reference-type variable to another **copies the reference, not the data**. Both variables then point to the *same* underlying object — changing the data through one variable is visible through the other. `string` cannot show this directly, because strings are immutable (every string operation returns a new string rather than modifying the original — the exception is explained below). The example uses a minimal preview of `class` syntax, covered fully in Chapter 12, purely to show the sharing behavior:

Two notes worth remembering:

- `struct` vs `class` is a common interview question because they look similar in code but behave differently: `struct` is a **value type** (copied), `class` is a **reference type** (shared) — exactly the `Box` example above, if `class Box` were changed to `struct Box`.
- `string` is the exception that proves confusing: it is *technically* a reference type, but because strings are immutable, it behaves like a value type in every practical sense. Reassigning a string variable always points it at a new string object rather than mutating the one already there, so you never observe the "shared object" behavior `Box` just demonstrated.

Here is the full comparison side by side:

| | **Value Types** | **Reference Types** |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Stored directly in the variable | Variable holds a reference to heap memory |
| Assignment | Copies the value | Copies the reference (both point to the same object) |
| Default value | `0` / `false` / `'\0'` | `null` |
| Built-in examples | `int`, `long`, `double`, `float`, `decimal`, `bool`, `char` | `string`, `object` |
| User-defined examples | `struct`, `enum`, `record struct` | `class`, `interface`, `delegate`, `record` |

```{index} void
```

#### `void`

`void` is a special case: it means "no type," used only as a method's return type to say the method does not return a value. You cannot declare a variable of type `void` — `void x;` is a compile-time error, because `void` describes an absence of a value, not a kind of value. You will use it constantly starting in Chapter 5, whenever a method's job is to *do* something (print output, modify state) rather than compute and return a result:

For now, recognize this distinction in built-in calls: `Math.Abs(-3)` produces a value that can be stored, while `Console.WriteLine("Hello")` prints a message and produces no result to assign. Defining a `void` method is taught in Chapter 5.

```{index} default value; default keyword
```

#### Default Values

Every type has a **default value** — the value a variable gets if C# has to fill it in without one you provided (for example, in an uninitialized array element, or a field you have not assigned in a constructor). The default value comes straight from the value-type/reference-type split above:

- Every value type defaults to some form of "zero": `0` for numeric types, `false` for `bool`, `'\0'` (the null character) for `char`.
- Every reference type defaults to `null` — no object yet, nothing to point to.

The `default` keyword asks for a type's default value directly, either as `default(int)` or, when C# can infer the type, just `default`:

Console.WriteLine(default(int));      // 0
Console.WriteLine(default(bool));     // False
Console.WriteLine(default(double));   // 0
Console.WriteLine(default(string) == null);  // True

int count = default;  // type inferred from the declaration
Console.WriteLine(count);

#### A Note on Unmanaged Types

C#'s reference documentation also names a category called **unmanaged types** — value types whose fields, all the way down, are themselves value types with no references anywhere inside them (`int`, a `struct` made only of `int` fields, and so on). The category exists because a small set of advanced features — interop with native code, and low-level performance-sensitive code using pointers — are restricted to types that satisfy this guarantee. You do not need to identify unmanaged types yourself in this book; it is mentioned here only so the term is not a surprise if you encounter it in official C# documentation or advanced references.

### Common Data Types in C\#

C# is a "strongly typed" language, meaning that every variable and constant has a type.
In addition to variables, types are also required for expressions that evaluate to a
value, method declarations with names, input parameters, and return values. Examples
of common value types (declared and initiated with value assignment) are as follows.

```csharp
int myNum = 5;                  // Integer (whole number)
long myNum = 15000000000L;      // Integer
double myDoubleNum = 5.99D;     // Floating point number
char myLetter = 'D';            // Character
bool myBool = true;             // Boolean
string myText = "Hello";        // String
```

From the list above you may notice that C# requires number **suffixes** for
numeric types. The purpose of using suffixes is to help the compiler unambiguously
identify the data type of the value/literal. The basic rules for integral
literal number suffixes are:

- If an integral literal has no suffix, its type is the first of the following types in
  which its value can be represented: int, uint, long, ulong.
- l or L for long
- U or u for unsigned integer
- UL or ul for unsigned long

For floating-point numeric types:

- The number literal without suffix or with the d or D suffix is of type double
- f or F suffix is of type float
- m or M suffix is of type decimal

A purpose of defining data types is for memory allocation. Examples of some
defined types and their memory size can be seen in the table below.

| No. | Group | Type | Size | Precision | Description |
|-----|-------|------|------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | **Integer** | `byte` | 1 byte/8 bits | | Integral range 0 to 255 (no negative values) |
| 2 | | `short` | 16 bits | | Integral range -32,768 to 32,767 |
| 3 |  | **\*** **`int`** | 4 bytes/32 bits | | Integral range -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 |
| 4 | | `long` | 8 bytes/64 bits | | Integral range -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 |
| 5 | **Floating Point** | **\*** `float` | 4 bytes/32 bits | ~6-9 digits | Fractional numbers |
| 6 |  | **`double`** | 8 bytes/64 bits | ~15-17 digits | Fractional numbers, general math |
| 7 | | `decimal` | 16 bytes/128 bits | 28-29 digits | Fractional numbers, high precision (use for money) |
| 8 | **Boolean** | **\*** **`bool`** | 1 bit | | True or false values |
| 9 | **Text** | `char` | 2 bytes | | Single character, single quotes `'A'` |
| 10 |  | **\*** **`string`** | 2 bytes per character | | Sequence of characters, double quotes `"Hello"` |

Choosing types is a design decision to meet the needs of different use scenarios.
For example, for financial unit, the *decimal* type may be a better choice because it
is designed for the purpose of holding a larger range of digits with higher precision.

One attribute of the integral value data types is that they can be either signed or
unsigned. A signed type uses its bytes to represent an equal number of positive
and negative numbers; whereas an unsigned type (such as `ushort`, `uint`,
and `ulong`) uses its bytes to represent only positive numbers. The difference between
singed and unsigned numbers can be seen from the example below:

Unsigned integral types:

### Data Types in Action

The following subsections explore each built-in type through examples you can
run with `csharprepl`, `Run C#`, or VS Code.

```{index} integer type; int; long; byte; sbyte
```

#### Integer Types

**Integer types** store whole numbers with no fractional part. The most common
choice is `int` (32-bit signed), which covers roughly ±2.1 billion. Use `long`
(64-bit) when you need a larger range, or `byte` for small non-negative values
(0–255).

Unsigned variants (`uint`, `ulong`, `ushort`, `byte`) hold only non-negative
values, which doubles the positive range but disallows negatives.

Numeric literals default to `int`. Use suffixes to specify other types:
`L`/`l` for `long`, `U`/`u` for `uint`, `UL`/`ul` for `ulong`.

```{index} floating-point type; float; double; decimal
```

#### Floating-Point Types

C# has three types for fractional numbers:

| Type | Size | Precision | Suffix | Use for |
|------|------|-----------|--------|---------|
| `float` | 32-bit | ~6–9 digits | `f` or `F` | Graphics, sensors |
| `double` | 64-bit | ~15–17 digits | `d` or `D` (default) | General math |
| `decimal` | 128-bit | 28–29 digits | `m` or `M` | Money, finance |

`double` is the default type for decimal literals. Use `decimal` whenever
rounding errors are unacceptable (e.g., currency); never use `float`/`double`
for money.

:::{important}
Floating-point arithmetic is approximate — `0.1 + 0.2` does not equal `0.3`
exactly in binary representation.

This is not a C# bug; it is a consequence of how computers store fractional
numbers. Memory stores bits (0s and 1s), so values are encoded in **base 2
(binary)**. Just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly in base 10 (0.3333…), many
decimal fractions — including 0.1 and 0.2 — cannot be represented exactly in
binary. The closest representable binary value is used instead, and when you
add two of these approximations the tiny errors accumulate, giving a result
like `0.30000000000000004` instead of `0.3`.

For money or anything where exact decimal rounding matters, use `decimal`,
which stores numbers in base 10 internally and avoids this problem entirely.
:::

```{index} boolean type; bool
```

#### Boolean (`bool`)

A `bool` holds exactly one of two values: `true` or `false`. It is the result
of any comparison or logical expression, and is the required type for `if`
conditions and loop guards.

Unlike C/C++, C# does **not** allow integers to be used as booleans — `if (1)`
is a compile-time error.

```{index} character type; char; Unicode
```

#### Character (`char`)

`char` represents a single Unicode UTF-16 character, written in **single
quotes**. Internally it is stored as a 16-bit unsigned integer, so it can be
cast to and from `int`. Common escape sequences:

| Sequence | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `'\n'` | Newline |
| `'\t'` | Tab |
| `'\\'` | Backslash |
| `'\''` | Single quote |

Note that `'A'` (char) is different from `"A"` (string of length 1).

```{index} string type; string interpolation; verbatim string
```

#### String (`string`)

`string` is a sequence of `char` values, written in **double quotes**. Strings
are **immutable** — operations like concatenation return a new string.

Key features:
- **Interpolation**: embed expressions with `$"...{expr}..."`
- **Verbatim literals**: prefix with `@` to treat backslashes literally (useful
  for file paths)
- **Common members**: `.Length`, `.ToUpper()`, `.ToLower()`, `.Contains()`,
  `.Substring()`, `.Replace()`, indexing with `[i]`

A string is a **sequence of characters** — each character has a numeric
index starting at `0`. For example, in `"formosa"`, `'f'` is at index 0
and `'a'` is at index 6. The last character is always at index `length - 1`.

| Index     | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|-----------|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Character | f | o | r | m | o | s | a |

When represented in code, indexing works like the example below.
string txt = "ilha formosa";
Console.WriteLine(txt[3]);

Note that, in the example above, the output is a character since strings consist of characters. Note that the `char` type literals are created by delimiting the characters by **single quotation** marks.

### Type Conversion

C# variables have specific types, but values sometimes need to move between
types. Type conversions are either **implicit** (automatic) or **explicit**
(manual cast required).

**Implicit casting** happens automatically when converting a smaller type to a
larger one — no data is lost:

```text
char → int → long → float → double
```

**Explicit casting** is required when converting a larger type to a smaller one,
because precision or range may be lost:

```text
double → float → long → int → char
```

For example:

```csharp
int a = 123;
long b = a;        // implicit: int fits in long, no cast needed
int c = (int) b;   // explicit: long → int, cast required
```

Use `GetType()` to inspect a variable's type at runtime. When types are *not*
cast properly, C# raises a compile-time error. For example, assigning a `double`
directly to an `int` fails:
double d = 2.0;
int i = d;
Note that if you choose to agree with the message and perform a type casting, you lose the
precision of `double` over an `int`.

double d = 2.5;       // create a double type variable d
Console.WriteLine(d);  // display the value of d

int i = default;       // explicitly ask for the default int value
Console.WriteLine(i);  // display the default value of an int

i = (int)d;            // explicitly tell the compiler you intend the conversion
Console.WriteLine(i);  // display i; the .5 is lost

## Follow a Value Through a Conversion

Suppose three employees share ten work hours. The expression `10 / 3` has two integer operands, so it produces the integer 3. Assigning that result to a double afterward produces 3.0; the missing fractional part cannot be recovered. Converting an operand before division changes which arithmetic operation is performed. This is the same evaluation-order reasoning used for ordinary expressions: work out each intermediate value and its type before considering the destination variable.

| Step | Value | Type | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read the literal 10 | 10 | int | Ten whole hours in this example |
| Evaluate 10 / 3 | 3 | int | Integer quotient |
| Convert that quotient | 3.0 | double | Conversion preserves the already truncated result |
| Evaluate 10.0 / 3 | approximately 3.3333 | double | Fractional division happened before assignment |

A cast is written `(DestinationType)expression`. The parentheses identify a requested conversion; they do not mean that conversion is lossless. Converting a floating-point value to an integer discards its fractional part within the supported range. Parsing is different: `int.Parse(text)` interprets a textual representation under a format contract. Neither a cast nor a parse proves the resulting business value is allowed. A successfully parsed negative package count may still violate the application rule.
